readSections: Foreword and Lecture 1 (introduction: Drinfeld's lemma, shtukas in mixed characteristic)
Lectures 2–5 (Huber rings, continuous valuations, rational subsets, (pre-)adic spaces with the appendix to Lecture 3, examples, analytic points, adic morphisms, sheafiness, Cartier divisors)
Lectures 6–7 (perfectoid rings, tilting, untilts, sousperfectoid rings, perfectoid spaces, almost purity, the étale site)

Lectures 8–10 (pro-étale morphisms, diamonds, descent, quasi-pro-étale maps, Spd ℚ_p, the functor X ↦ X^♦, underlying spaces and étale sites), with the appendix to Lecture 10 (cohomology of local systems)

summary: Scholze and Weinstein's lectures build, from Huber's adic spaces through perfectoid spaces, diamonds and the v-topology, the moduli spaces of mixed-characteristic local shtukas Sht_{𝒢,b,{μ_i}} for any reductive group, any σ-conjugacy class b and any collection of cocharacters, prove that they are locally spatial diamonds with étale period maps to twisted Beilinson–Drinfeld Grassmannians (Theorem 23.1.4, Corollary 23.5.3), and identify the one-leg minuscule case with local Shimura varieties and, for EL/PEL data, with the generic fibres of Rapoport–Zink spaces (Theorem 24.2.5, Corollary 24.3.5). Along the way they give: the local Drinfeld lemma π_1((Spd ℚ_p)^n/p.Fr.) = G_{ℚ_p}^n (Theorem 16.3.1); Fargues' classification of shtukas with one leg and of p-divisible groups over 𝒪_C and over integral perfectoid rings by Breuil–Kisin–Fargues modules (Theorems 14.1.1, 14.4.1, 17.5.2), with Kedlaya's extension of bundles from 𝒴 to Spec A_inf; the B_dR⁺-affine Grassmannian, its Schubert varieties and Demazure resolutions, and its Beilinson–Drinfeld deformation to the Witt vector affine Grassmannian, ind-proper by Anschütz's theorem (Lectures 19–21); a conjecture on the existence of local models (Conjecture 21.4.1) with the examples of Rapoport–Zink and Kudla–Rapoport–Zink; integral models M^int_{(𝒢,b,μ)} as v-sheaves and their identification with Rapoport–Zink formal schemes (Theorem 25.1.2), proving the RZ17 and KRZ conjectures on Drinfeld's moduli problem (Theorems 25.4.1, 25.5.2). The atlas plans most of this: the Tau Ceti AdicSpaces roadmap (Layers 0–6, with Tau Ceti library code for Huber rings, Spa, rational subsets, analytic points and open mapping), AdicSpacesPartII and AdicEtaleGeometry, PerfectoidSpaces P0–P7, DiamondsAndVStacks D0–D6 and DiamondEtaleCohomology, RelativeFarguesFontaine, FarguesFontaineDiamonds, VectorBundlesAndIsocrystals, BunGAndNewtonStrata, GeometricSatakeAndFusion GS0 (which already cites these lectures), HeckeStacksAndLocalShtukas HS0/HS2, AInfCohomology AI.2 (Fargues' equivalence), VStackSheavesAndLisseCategories VS1 and GlobalShtukas GS.2/GS.4. What is missing is routed to five Part IIs that coalesce with pending candidates (prismatic Dieudonné theory; integral recovery for diamonds; local models; integral parahoric models and Rapoport–Zink spaces; mod-p cohomology of proper smooth rigid spaces) and three sources of existing layers (VB3–VB4, RF0:integral-Y, HS2). Six misprints are recorded.

items.name: Definition 1.1.1: Drinfeld's shtukas of rank n over a scheme over F_p
items.statement: Let X/𝔽_p be a smooth projective curve. A shtuka of rank n over an 𝔽_p-scheme S is a pair (ℰ, φ_ℰ) with ℰ a rank-n vector bundle on S ×_{𝔽_p} X and φ_ℰ : Frob_S^*ℰ ⇢ ℰ a meromorphic isomorphism, defined on an open U ⊂ S ×_{𝔽_p} X that is fibrewise dense in X; Frob_S is the product of the p-th power Frobenius of S with the identity of X. Over an algebraically closed field its legs x_1, …, x_m are the points where φ_ℰ is undefined, and at each leg its behaviour is a conjugacy class μ_i of cocharacters 𝔾_m → GL_n.
items.note: GlobalShtukasAndFunctionFieldLanglands GS.2 defines multi-leg global shtukas as successive modifications with a Frobenius isomorphism; Lecture 11 (Definition 11.1.1) restates this with legs and graphs.

items.name: Lemma 1.1.2 (Drinfeld's lemma, as used for shtukas)
items.statement: For a dense open U ⊂ X of the curve, the natural map π_1(U^m / partial Frob.) → π_1(U) × ⋯ × π_1(U) (m copies) is an isomorphism; consequently a ℚ_ℓ-local system on U^m with commuting isomorphisms F_i^*L ≅ L (partial Frobenii) is a representation of π_1(U)^m. (Remark 1.1.3: the sheaf R^d(f_N)_!ℚ_ℓ on the shtuka space is not constructible, and Drinfeld works with a bounded variant, lisse on (X∖N)^m.)
items.note: GS.4 'Partial Frobenius and Drinfeld lemma'. The scheme statement in full generality is Theorem 16.2.4 below.

items.name: Definition 1.2.1 and Theorem 1.2.2: the local Drinfeld lemma for Spa ℚ_p × Spa ℚ_p
items.statement: Let Spa ℚ_p × Spa ℚ_p := D̃*_{ℚ_p}/ℤ_p^× (formally), with the operator φ given by p ∈ ℚ_p^×, and X = (D̃*_{ℚ_p}/ℤ_p^×)/φ^ℤ = D̃*_{ℚ_p}/ℚ_p^×, where D̃*_{ℚ_p} is the punctured perfectoid open unit disc; finite étale covers of X are ℚ_p^×-equivariant finite étale covers of D̃*_{ℚ_p}, with profinite group π_1(X). Then π_1(X) ≅ Gal(ℚ̄_p/ℚ_p) × Gal(ℚ̄_p/ℚ_p). Similarly for K = 𝔽_p((t)), X = D*_K/φ^ℤ has π_1(X) ≅ Gal(K̄/K) × Gal(K̄/K).
items.note: Made precise as Theorem 15.1.1 and, for any number of factors, Theorem 16.3.1; VStackSheavesAndLisseCategories VS1 plans Drinfeld's lemma for the diamond products (FS IV.7).

items.name: Lemma 2.1.1 (Stacks 00M9): completions along a finitely generated ideal
items.statement: Let A be a ring, M an A-module and I ⊂ A a finitely generated ideal. For the I-adic completion M̂ = lim M/I^nM one has M̂/IM̂ = M/IM, and M̂ is I-adically complete. The lemma fails in general if I is not finitely generated.
items.locator: Lecture 2, §2.1, Lemma 2.1.1 (in a footnote continuing onto p. 8), p. 7
items.note: Mathlib/RingTheory/AdicCompletion/Completeness.lean: isAdicComplete (h : I.FG) : IsAdicComplete I (AdicCompletion I M) (Stacks 05GG(1)); pow_smul_top_eq_ker_eval identifies I^n • M̂ with the kernel of evaluation to M/I^nM for I finitely generated.

items.name: Formal schemes and rigid-analytic spaces (the motivating categories of §2.1)
items.statement: An adic ring is a topological ring carrying the I-adic topology for an ideal of definition I; Spf A is the set of open prime ideals with basic opens D(f) and 𝒪_{Spf A}(D(f)) the I-adic completion of A[f^{-1}]; a formal scheme is a topologically ringed space locally of the form Spf A (here with finitely generated ideals of definition). For a nonarchimedean field K, the Tate algebra K⟨T_1, …, T_n⟩ is the completion of K[T_1, …, T_n] in the Gauss norm, a K-affinoid algebra is a quotient of one, rational domains U(f_1, …, f_n/g) ⊂ MaxSpec A (f_i, g generating the unit ideal) form a G-topology with a sheaf of K-algebras, and rigid-analytic spaces are G-ringed spaces locally isomorphic to K-affinoid spaces. The rigid open unit disc {|T| < 1} ⊂ MaxSpec ℚ_p⟨T⟩ is not affinoid but the ascending union of the U(T^n/p).
items.note: AdicSpacesPartII R2 (formal schemes and generic fibres) and R1 (analytification); the Tau Ceti AdicSpaces Layer 5 examples include the open unit disc as a union of rational discs.

items.name: Definition 2.2.1, Definition 2.2.5 and Example 2.2.2: Huber rings, rings and ideals of definition, Tate rings and pseudo-uniformizers
items.statement: A topological ring A is Huber if it has an open subring A_0 that is adic for a finitely generated ideal I ⊂ A_0 (the I^n form a basis of neighbourhoods of 0); A_0 is a ring of definition (not assumed complete) and I an ideal of definition. The completion Â is Huber with Â = Â_0 ⊗_{A_0} A. A Huber ring is Tate if it contains a topologically nilpotent unit, a pseudo-uniformizer. Discrete rings, adic rings with finitely generated ideal of definition, and A_0[g^{-1}] with the g-adic topology (g a nonzero-divisor) are Huber; ℚ_p and ℚ_p⟨T⟩ are Tate, ℤ_p and ℤ_p[[T]] are not.
items.locator: Lecture 2, §2.2, Definition 2.2.1, Example 2.2.2 and Definition 2.2.5, pp. 9–10
items.note: TauCeti/RingTheory/Huber/Basic.lean: PairOfDefinition (open subring with a finitely generated ideal whose adic topology is the subspace topology), IsHuberRing (a pair of definition exists), IsTateRing extends IsHuberRing with a pseudouniformiser (IsPseudoUniformizer a := IsUnit a ∧ IsTopologicallyNilpotent a); Padic/Basic.lean and Padic/Field.lean give the ℤ_p, ℚ_p examples. Completion: TauCeti/RingTheory/Huber/Completion.lean.

items.name: Definition 2.2.3, Lemma 2.2.4 and Proposition 2.2.6: bounded subsets and rings of definition
items.statement: A subset S of a topological ring A is bounded if for every neighbourhood U of 0 there is a neighbourhood V of 0 with VS ⊂ U. A subring A_0 of a Huber ring is a ring of definition iff it is open and bounded (2.2.4). (2.2.6) (1) A = A_0[g^{-1}] with the g-adic topology is Tate. (2) If A is Tate with pseudo-uniformizer g and A_0 a ring of definition, then g^n ∈ A_0 for n large, A_0 is g^n-adic and A = A_0[(g^n)^{-1}]. (3) In that situation S ⊂ A is bounded iff S ⊂ g^{-n}A_0 for some n.
items.locator: Lecture 2, §2.2, Definition 2.2.3, Lemma 2.2.4 and Proposition 2.2.6, pp. 10–11
items.note: Tau Ceti has IsBounded (TauCeti/RingTheory/Huber/Bounded.lean: ∀ U ∈ 𝓝 0, ∃ V ∈ 𝓝 0, V * S ⊆ U) and isBounded_of_isAdic (RingOfDefinition.lean), and IsTateRing.exists_hasBasis_nhds_zero; the Tau Ceti AdicSpaces Layer 0 plans Wedhorn Lemma 6.2 (rings of definition = open bounded adic subrings) and the Tate-ring statements in full.

items.name: Definition 2.2.8, Proposition 2.2.10 and Definition 2.2.11: power-bounded elements A°, and uniform Huber rings
items.statement: x ∈ A is power-bounded if {x^n : n ≥ 0} is bounded; A° ⊂ A is the subring of power-bounded elements. Every ring of definition lies in A°, and A° is the filtered union of the rings of definition. A Huber ring is uniform if A° is bounded (equivalently a ring of definition); a separated uniform Tate ring is reduced. (Example 2.2.9: ℚ_p⟨T⟩° = ℤ_p⟨T⟩, while for ℚ_p[T]/T², A° = ℤ_p ⊕ ℚ_pT is unbounded.)
items.locator: Lecture 2, §2.2, Definition 2.2.8, Example 2.2.9, Proposition 2.2.10 and Definition 2.2.11, pp. 11–12
items.note: Library pieces: tauceti:TauCeti.Huber.IsPowerBounded and TauCeti.Huber.powerBoundedSubring (PowerBounded.lean, Wedhorn Proposition 5.30), IsBounded.isPowerBounded_of_mem. Layer 0 plans 'A° is the union of the rings of definition' (Wedhorn Corollary 6.4); uniformity (Hansen–Kedlaya Definition 2.3) is Layer 4.2.

items.name: Remark 2.2.7: analytic Huber rings
items.statement: A Huber ring A is analytic (Kedlaya) if the ideal generated by its topologically nilpotent elements is the unit ideal. Tate rings are analytic; the converse fails (Kedlaya, Example 1.5.7).
items.note: AdicEtaleGeometry A1 packet node yoneda-adic-analytic-tate-local, with Proposition 4.3.1.

items.name: Definition 2.2.12: rings of integral elements and Huber pairs
items.statement: A subring A⁺ ⊂ A of a Huber ring is a ring of integral elements if it is open, integrally closed in A, and A⁺ ⊂ A°; a Huber pair is (A, A⁺) with A Huber and A⁺ a ring of integral elements. The topologically nilpotent elements A°° always lie in A⁺.
items.note: TauCeti/RingTheory/Huber/Pair.lean: IsRingOfIntegralElements (open, integrally closed, ≤ powerBoundedSubring), Pair (a Huber ring with such a subring); the lemma after IsRingOfIntegralElements proves that an open integrally closed subring contains every topologically nilpotent element.

items.name: Definition 2.3.1: continuous valuations and their equivalence
items.statement: A continuous valuation on a topological ring A is |·| : A → Γ ∪ {0}, Γ a totally ordered abelian group (written multiplicatively), with |ab| = |a||b|, |a + b| ≤ max(|a|, |b|), |1| = 1, |0| = 0, and {a : |a| < γ} open for every γ in the image. Two are equivalent if |a| ≥ |b| ⟺ |a|′ ≥ |b|′; then the value groups generated by the images are isomorphic compatibly. The kernel is a prime ideal.
items.note: As in PAPER-SCHOLZE-12 items 7 and 9; ValuationSpectrum.cont is the continuous locus Cont A.

items.name: Definition 2.3.2 and Theorem 2.3.3: the adic spectrum Spa(A, A⁺) and its spectrality
items.statement: Spa(A, A⁺) is the set of equivalence classes of continuous valuations |·| on A with |A⁺| ≤ 1, topologized by the sets {x : |f(x)| ≤ |g(x)| ≠ 0}, f, g ∈ A. It is a spectral space (Huber 1993, Theorem 3.5(i)).
items.note: TauCeti/AlgebraicGeometry/AdicSpace/Spa/Basic.lean (spa Aplus := cont A ∩ {v : ∀ a ∈ Aplus, v a ≤ 1}) and Spa/Spectral.lean (SpectralSpace (spa Aplus) from a pair of definition, Wedhorn Theorem 7.35).

items.name: Definition 2.3.4: spectral spaces (Hochster)
items.statement: A topological space T is spectral if the following equivalent conditions hold: (1) T ≅ Spec R for a ring R; (2) T is an inverse limit of finite T_0 spaces; (3) T is quasicompact, has a basis of quasicompact opens stable under finite intersections, and is sober. (Example 2.3.5: Spec ℤ ≅ lim T_i for finite T_0 spaces T_i.)
items.note: Mathlib/Topology/Spectral/Basic.lean defines SpectralSpace by condition (3) (T0, compact, quasi-sober, quasi-separated, prespectral). The equivalence with (1) and (2) (Hochster) is not in the library; it is not used later in the book.

items.name: Examples 2.3.6–2.3.8: the points of Spa(ℤ, ℤ), of the adic closed unit disc, and Zariski–Riemann spaces
items.statement: Spa(ℤ, ℤ) has the generic point η, a closed point s_p for each prime and points η_p (the p-adic valuation) with closure {η_p, s_p}; for discrete R there are continuous maps Spec R → Spa(R, R) → Spec R composing to the identity. For K algebraically closed, spherically complete with value group ℝ_{>0}, the points of Spa(K⟨T⟩, 𝒪_K⟨T⟩) are the classical points, the Gauss points x_r and the rank-2 points x_{r±}. For a discrete field K and A ⊂ K, Spa(K, A) is homeomorphic to the Zariski–Riemann space Zar(K, A).
items.locator: Lecture 2, §2.3, Example 2.3.6, Example 2.3.7 and Example 2.3.8, pp. 14–16
items.note: The Tau Ceti AdicSpaces Layer 5 examples (Spa(K, K°), closed discs) and tauceti:TauCeti.ValuationSpectrum.classicalPoint, closedPolydisc (Spa/Polydisc.lean) cover the disc; the full classification of disc points is a planned example, not library.

items.name: Propositions 2.3.9–2.3.10: completion and the size of Spa
items.statement: (2.3.9) For the completion (Â, Â⁺) of a Huber pair, Spa(Â, Â⁺) ≅ Spa(A, A⁺) (Huber 1993, 3.9). (2.3.10) For a complete Huber pair: (1) if A ≠ 0 then Spa(A, A⁺) ≠ ∅; (2) A⁺ = {f ∈ A : |f(x)| ≤ 1 for all x}; (3) f ∈ A is invertible iff |f(x)| ≠ 0 for all x.
items.note: Library for 2.3.10, as in PAPER-SCHOLZE-12/16: tauceti:TauCeti.ValuationSpectrum.spa_eq_empty_iff_subsingleton_quotient_closure_zero, mem_iff_forall_vle_one, isUnit_iff_forall_mem_spa_notMem_supp. The completion homeomorphism 2.3.9 is planned in Layer 2/3 (Tau Ceti has only the separation-quotient homeomorphism spaSeparationQuotientHomeomorph).

items.name: Definition 3.1.1 and Proposition 3.1.2: rational subsets and their intersections
items.statement: For s ∈ A and finite T ⊂ A with TA open, U(T/s) = {x : |t(x)| ≤ |s(x)| ≠ 0 for all t ∈ T}; rational subsets are open, and a finite intersection of rational subsets is rational.
items.note: Spa/RationalSubset/Basic.lean: rationalSubset Aplus T s := spa Aplus ∩ basicOpenFinset T s, and rationalSubset_inter : R(T₁/s₁) ∩ R(T₂/s₂) = R((insert s₁ T₁ * insert s₂ T₂)/(s₁s₂)).

items.name: Theorem 3.1.3 with Lemmas 3.1.4–3.1.5: rational localization and its universal property
items.statement: For a rational subset U ⊂ Spa(A, A⁺) there is a complete Huber pair (A, A⁺) → (𝒪_X(U), 𝒪_X⁺(U)) such that Spa(𝒪_X(U), 𝒪_X⁺(U)) → Spa(A, A⁺) factors over U and is universal for such maps; it is a homeomorphism onto U, so U is quasicompact (Huber 1994, 1.3). The construction topologizes A[1/s] with ring of definition A_0[t/s : t ∈ T] (Lemma 3.1.4), using that TA open implies TA_0 open (Lemma 3.1.5).
items.locator: Lecture 3, §3.1, Theorem 3.1.3, Lemma 3.1.4 and Lemma 3.1.5, p. 18
items.note: Library pieces: tauceti:TauCeti.Huber.PairOfDefinition.completionLocalization (the completed localisation topology, LocalizationTopology/Completion.lean) and tauceti:TauCeti.ValuationSpectrum.spaLocalizationHomeomorph (Spa/Localization/Homeomorph.lean, homeomorphism onto the rational subset); the Tau Ceti AdicSpaces Layer 3.1 plans the universal property and the plus ring A_U⁺ as a whole.

items.name: Definition 3.1.6, Proposition 3.1.7 and Definition 3.1.11: the structure presheaves 𝒪_X, 𝒪_X⁺ and sheafy pairs
items.statement: 𝒪_X(U) is as in Theorem 3.1.3 for rational U and 𝒪_X(W) = lim_{U ⊂ W rational} 𝒪_X(U) for open W; similarly 𝒪_X⁺. For all U, 𝒪_X⁺(U) = {f ∈ 𝒪_X(U) : |f(x)| ≤ 1 for x ∈ U}, so 𝒪_X⁺ is a sheaf if 𝒪_X is. A Huber pair is sheafy if 𝒪_X is a sheaf of topological rings (then so is 𝒪_X⁺).
items.locator: Lecture 3, §3.1, Definition 3.1.6, Proposition 3.1.7 and Definition 3.1.11, p. 19
items.note: Library piece: tauceti:TauCeti.ValuationSpectrum.presentationLimitPresheaf (Spa/StructurePresheaf/Basic.lean); Layer 3.3 plans 𝒪_X and 𝒪_X⁺, Layer 4 sheafiness (Huber.IsSheafyPair). AdicEtaleGeometry A1 node huber-pair-rational-site.

items.name: Theorem 3.1.8 with Example 3.1.9 and Remark 3.1.10: Huber's sheafiness criteria
items.statement: For a complete Huber pair (A, A⁺), 𝒪_X is a sheaf of topological rings if (1) A is discrete, (2) A is finitely generated over a noetherian ring of definition, or (3) A is Tate and strongly noetherian (all A⟨T_1, …, T_n⟩ noetherian) (Huber 1994, 2.2). ℂ_p is covered by (3), not (2). Rost's examples show 𝒪_X need not be a sheaf.
items.locator: Lecture 3, §3.1, Theorem 3.1.8, Example 3.1.9 and Remark 3.1.10, p. 19
items.note: Layer 4.1 plans case (3) through Wedhorn Theorem 8.28; tauceti:TauCeti.Huber.IsStronglyNoetherian is the library notion (StronglyNoetherian.lean).

items.name: Definition 3.2.1 and Proposition 3.2.2: the category (V) and adic spaces
items.statement: (V) has objects (X, 𝒪_X, (|·(x)|)_{x ∈ X}) with X a topological space, 𝒪_X a sheaf of topological rings and |·(x)| an equivalence class of continuous valuations on 𝒪_{X,x}; morphisms are continuous maps of topologically ringed spaces compatible with the valuations. An adic space is an object covered by Spa(A_i, A_i⁺) with (A_i, A_i⁺) sheafy. The functor (A, A⁺) ↦ Spa(A, A⁺) from sheafy complete Huber pairs to adic spaces is fully faithful (Huber 1994, 2.1).
items.note: Tau Ceti AdicSpaces Layer 5 ('An affinoid adic space is an object of 𝒱 isomorphic to the pre-adic spectrum of a sheafy Huber pair'); AdicEtaleGeometry A1 node adic-spaces-in-yoneda-adic-spaces.

items.name: Proposition 3.3.1: Cont(A) and the role of A⁺
items.statement: (1) Cont(A), the space of continuous valuations with the topology generated by {|f| ≤ |g| ≠ 0}, is spectral. (2) Subsets of the form ⋂_{f ∈ S}{|f| ≤ 1}, S ⊂ A°, correspond bijectively to open integrally closed subrings A⁺ ⊂ A°, via F ↦ {f : |f(x)| ≤ 1 on F} and A⁺ ↦ {x : |f(x)| ≤ 1 for f ∈ A⁺} (Huber 1993, 3.2, 3.3). A⁺ is needed because Cont(B) of a rational localization is larger than U, and A⁺ = A° is not stable under rational localization.
items.note: Part (1) is library: tauceti:TauCeti.ValuationSpectrum.spectralSpace_cont_of_pairOfDefinition (Cont/Spectral.lean, Wedhorn Corollary 7.12). Part (2) is planned in Layers 1–2 (Proposition 7.52(1) is library as mem_iff_forall_vle_one).

items.name: Definition 3.4.1 with the Appendix to Lecture 3 (Definitions 3.5.1–3.5.2, Proposition 3.5.3): pre-adic spaces
items.statement: For a sheaf F on CAff^op (complete Huber pairs with the analytic topology), F → Spa^Y(A, A⁺) is an open immersion if F = colim_{V ⊂ U rational} Spa^Y(𝒪_X(V), 𝒪_X⁺(V)) for an open U ⊂ Spa(A, A⁺); a pre-adic space is a sheaf F = colim_{Spa^Y(A,A⁺) ⊂ F} Spa^Y(A, A⁺). Equivalently (appendix) a pre-adic space is an object of (V)^ind (sheaves of ind-topological rings) locally isomorphic to Spa^ind(A, A⁺), the sheafification of 𝒪_X in ind-topological rings; the two notions are equivalent compatibly with open immersions, and adic spaces form a full subcategory.
items.locator: Lecture 3, §3.4, Definition 3.4.1, Definition 3.5.2 and Proposition 3.5.3 with Definition 3.5.1 (p. 23), pp. 22–24
items.note: AdicEtaleGeometry A1 nodes generalized-adic-presentation, yoneda-adic-open-immersions and yoneda-adic-ind-ringed-description.

items.name: §4.1–4.2: Spa ℤ_p[[T]], its analytic locus 𝒴 and the radius map κ (Proposition 4.2.6)
items.statement: X = Spa(ℤ_p[[T]], ℤ_p[[T]]) has a unique non-analytic point x_{𝔽_p}; on 𝒴 = X ∖ {x_{𝔽_p}}, |T(x)| and |p(x)| are not both 0. There is a unique continuous map κ : |𝒴| → [0, ∞] with κ(x) = r iff |T(x)|^n ≥ |p(x)|^m for rational m/n > r and |T(x)|^n ≤ |p(x)|^m for m/n < r; κ is surjective. (§4.1 records the basic examples: points, discs, Spa ℤ_p, Spa ℚ_p, Spa(ℤ_p[[T]]) and Spa ℤ_p[[T]]⟨p/T⟩[1/T].)
items.note: The Tau Ceti AdicSpaces Layer 6.2 defines κ order-theoretically on the analytic open 𝒴 ⊂ Spa A_inf with κ(φv) = pκ(v); RelativeFarguesFontaine RF0:integral-Y covers it by |π|^n ≤ |[ϖ]| ≠ 0. Proposition 4.2.6 is the same construction for ℤ_p[[T]].

items.name: Definition 4.2.1 and Lemma 4.2.2: analytic points and their rank-one value
items.statement: A point x ∈ Spa(A, A⁺) is non-analytic if ker|·|_x is open, otherwise analytic. If x is analytic there is f in an ideal of definition with γ = |f(x)| ≠ 0 and γ^n → 0 cofinally; for a totally ordered abelian group Γ and γ < 1 with this cofinality there is a unique order-preserving homomorphism Γ → ℝ_{>0} sending γ to 1/2.
items.note: Library pieces: tauceti:TauCeti.ValuationSpectrum.IsAnalyticPoint (Spa/Analytic.lean: support not open), IsAnalyticPoint.isMicrobial and isAnalyticPoint_of_isTateRing. The rank-one homomorphism of Lemma 4.2.2 is planned in Layer 2 (analytic points), not in the library.

items.name: Definitions 4.2.3–4.2.4 and Proposition 4.2.5: nonarchimedean fields, affinoid fields, and points as maps to affinoid fields
items.statement: A nonarchimedean field is a complete nondiscrete topological field with a nonarchimedean norm. For analytic x, K(x) is the completion of Frac(A/ker|·|_x), a nonarchimedean field; at non-analytic points K(x) is discrete; x gives an open bounded valuation subring K(x)⁺. An affinoid field is a Huber pair (K, K⁺) with K nonarchimedean or discrete and K⁺ an open bounded valuation subring. Points of Spa(A, A⁺) correspond to maps (A, A⁺) → (K, K⁺) to affinoid fields with dense image of Frac; for analytic x, generalizations correspond to the K(y)⁺ ⊃ K(x)⁺, a chain whose maximal element is the rank-one valuation (Huber 1996, pp. 40–41).
items.locator: Lecture 4, §4.2, Definition 4.2.3, Definition 4.2.4 and Proposition 4.2.5, pp. 29–30
items.note: ClassicalAdicEtaleCohomology H2 nodes connectedness-via-maximal-generalisations and surjectivity-criterion-for-field-pair-extensions; nonarchimedean fields themselves are in Mathlib (NontriviallyNormedField, IsUltrametricDist; see PAPER-SCHOLZE-12/6); residue fields: tauceti:TauCeti.ValuationSpectrum.residueFieldValuation.

items.name: Proposition 4.3.1 and Definition 4.3.2: analytic points are locally Tate
items.statement: For a complete Huber pair: (1) A is analytic iff all points of Spa(A, A⁺) are analytic; (2) x is analytic iff it has a rational neighbourhood U with 𝒪_X(U) Tate. A point of a pre-adic space is analytic if it has an affinoid neighbourhood Spa(A, A⁺) with A Tate, and a pre-adic space is analytic if all its points are.
items.note: AdicEtaleGeometry A1 node yoneda-adic-analytic-tate-local. Library pieces: tauceti:TauCeti.ValuationSpectrum.isTateRing_completion_locTopology_of_mem_generators and spaAnalytic_eq_spa_of_isTateRing.

items.name: Proposition 4.3.3: maps of analytic pre-adic spaces are generalizing, and quasicompact surjections are quotient maps
items.statement: For a map f : Y → X of analytic pre-adic spaces, |f| is generalizing; if f is quasicompact and surjective, |f| is a quotient map.
items.note: DiamondsAndVStacks D0 plans ECD §2's quotient criteria for spectral maps (ECD Lemma 2.5); Proposition 17.1.2 uses this for v-covers.

items.name: Proposition 4.3.4: Banach's open mapping theorem over analytic Huber rings
items.statement: If A is an analytic Huber ring and M, N complete Banach A-modules, every continuous surjection M → N is open (Huber 1993, 2.4(i)).
items.note: The Tate case is library: tauceti:TauCeti.Huber.IsTateRing.isOpenMap (TauCeti/RingTheory/Huber/OpenMapping.lean: a surjective A-linear map continuous at 0 is open). The analytic, non-Tate case is AdicSpacesPartII R0 (node completed-tensor-banach-module) and Layer 0.

items.name: Definition 5.1.1, Lemma 5.1.2, Proposition 5.1.3 and Definition 5.1.4: adic and analytic morphisms
items.statement: A morphism A → B of Huber rings is adic if for compatible rings of definition A_0 → B_0 and an ideal of definition I, f(I)B_0 is an ideal of definition; a morphism of pairs is adic if the ring map is. If A is Tate every map A → B is adic; a map of complete Huber pairs is adic iff Spa(B, B⁺) → Spa(A, A⁺) sends analytic points to analytic points (Huber 1993, 3.8); so maps from analytic A are adic. A map of pre-adic spaces is analytic if it preserves analytic points.
items.locator: Lecture 5, §5.1, Definition 5.1.1, Lemma 5.1.2, Proposition 5.1.3 and Definition 5.1.4, p. 35
items.note: AdicEtaleGeometry A1 node yoneda-adic-analytic-tate-local.

items.name: Proposition 5.1.5 and Remarks 5.1.6–5.1.7: pushouts of Huber pairs along adic maps
items.statement: (1) Pullback along an adic map preserves rational subsets. (2) For adic maps (B, B⁺) ← (A, A⁺) → (C, C⁺) with compatible rings of definition and ideal of definition I, D = B ⊗_A C with ring of definition the image D_0 of B_0 ⊗_{A_0} C_0 and ideal ID_0, and D⁺ the integral closure of the image of B⁺ ⊗_{A⁺} C⁺, is a Huber pair and the pushout; after completion it is the pushout of complete pairs and Spa(D, D⁺) = Spa(B, B⁺) ×_{Spa(A,A⁺)} Spa(C, C⁺). The non-adic diagram (ℤ_p[[T]], ℤ_p[[T]]) ← (ℤ_p, ℤ_p) → (ℚ_p, ℤ_p) has no pushout.
items.locator: Lecture 5, §5.1, Proposition 5.1.5, Remark 5.1.6 and Remark 5.1.7, pp. 35–36
items.note: AdicEtaleGeometry A0/A1 (node yoneda-adic-fibre-products), whose canonical owner of completed tensor products is AdicSpacesPartII's foundational prefix (R0).

items.name: Theorem 5.2.1, Remark 5.2.2 and Corollary 5.2.3: uniform rings embed into products of residue fields (Berkovich)
items.statement: For A uniform (analytic), A → ∏_{x ∈ Spa(A,A⁺)} K(x) is a homeomorphism onto its image, and A° = {f : f ∈ 𝒪_{K(x)} for all x}; hence A → H^0(X, 𝒪̃_X) is injective for the sheafification 𝒪̃_X.
items.locator: Lecture 5, §5.2, Theorem 5.2.1, Remark 5.2.2 and Corollary 5.2.3, pp. 36–37
items.note: Layer 4.2 (stably uniform Tate rings, Hansen–Kedlaya) and AdicSpacesPartII R3 node stably-uniform-sheafy.

items.name: Definition 5.2.4, Theorem 5.2.5, Theorem 5.2.6 and Lemma 5.2.7: stably uniform pairs are sheafy, and sheafy analytic pairs are acyclic
items.statement: A complete analytic Huber pair is stably uniform if 𝒪_X(U) is uniform for all rational U. Stably uniform pairs are sheafy (Buzzard–Verberkmoes, Kedlaya–Liu 2.8.10, Mihara, Kedlaya). If a complete analytic pair is sheafy then H^i(X, 𝒪_X) = 0 for i > 0 (Kedlaya–Liu 2.4.23), reduced to simple Laurent covers X = {|f| ≤ 1} ∪ {|f| ≥ 1}, with Čech complex 0 → A → A⟨T⟩/(T − f) ⊕ A⟨S⟩/(Sf − 1) → A⟨T, T^{-1}⟩/(T − f) → 0; the last map is surjective, and if A is uniform the ideals are closed and the kernel is A (Lemma 5.2.7).
items.locator: Lecture 5, §5.2, Definition 5.2.4, Theorem 5.2.5, Theorem 5.2.6 and Lemma 5.2.7, p. 37
items.note: Layer 4.2 (stable uniformity ⇒ sheafiness, Buzzard–Verberkmoes) and Layer 4.1 (Laurent-cover exactness, Wedhorn Lemma 8.33); AdicSpacesPartII R3 plans acyclicity for affinoid covers ('the affinoid coherent-sheaf equivalence, acyclicity').

items.name: Theorem 5.2.8 and Lemma 5.2.9: vector bundles on sheafy analytic affinoids, and Beauville–Laszlo gluing
items.statement: For a sheafy analytic Huber pair, finite projective A-modules are equivalent to locally finite free 𝒪_X-modules (Kedlaya–Liu 2.7.7). (5.2.9, Beauville–Laszlo) For a ring R, a nonzero-divisor f and the f-adic completion R̂, R-modules without f-torsion are equivalent to triples (M_{R̂}, M_{R[f^{-1}]}, β) with β : M_{R̂}[f^{-1}] ≅ M_{R[f^{-1}]} ⊗_R R̂; M is finite projective iff both pieces are.
items.note: AdicSpacesPartII R3 (locally free sheaves on affinoids); RelativeFarguesFontaine RF4:vector-bundles node beauville-laszlo-module-gluing.

items.name: Definitions 5.3.1–5.3.2, 5.3.5 and 5.3.7 with Propositions 5.3.3, 5.3.4 and 5.3.8: Cartier divisors, meromorphy and closed Cartier divisors on uniform analytic adic spaces
items.statement: An adic space is uniform if 𝒪_X(U) is uniform on affinoid opens. On a uniform analytic X a Cartier divisor is an invertible ideal sheaf ℐ ⊂ 𝒪_X; for stably uniform (R, R⁺) its support is nowhere dense and Cartier divisors correspond to invertible ideals I ⊂ R with nowhere dense vanishing locus (5.3.3). With U = X ∖ Z there are injections 𝒪_X ↪ colim_n ℐ^{⊗−n} ↪ j_*𝒪_U, and f ∈ H^0(U, 𝒪_U) is meromorphic along ℐ if it lifts to H^0(X, colim ℐ^{⊗−n}) (depending on ℐ, not only its support, Remark 5.3.6). ℐ is closed if (Z, 𝒪_X/ℐ, valuations) is an adic space, iff ℐ(U) → 𝒪_X(U) has closed image on all affinoids; then U ∩ Z = Spa(R/I, integral closure of R⁺) (5.3.8). (Remark 5.3.9: closedness of fA ⊂ A for a regular f does not suffice; the Hodge–Tate period function on 𝒳*_{Γ(p^∞)}(ε)_a is an example.)
items.locator: Lecture 5, §5.3, Definition 5.3.1, Definition 5.3.2, Proposition 5.3.3, Proposition 5.3.4, Definition 5.3.5, Remark 5.3.6, Definition 5.3.7, Proposition 5.3.8 and Remark 5.3.9, pp. 38–40
items.note: RelativeFarguesFontaine RF2:untilts ('Prove injectivity and closed image of multiplication by a local generator … descend the Cartier divisor') and FarguesFontaineDiamonds F4 ('Prove it is a closed Cartier divisor'); the general notions are used by Definitions 11.1.2 and 11.4.1 for meromorphy along the legs.

items.name: Definition 6.1.1, Remark 6.1.3 and Definition 6.1.7: perfectoid Tate rings and perfectoid fields
items.statement: A complete Tate ring R is perfectoid if it is uniform and has a pseudo-uniformizer ϖ with ϖ^p | p in R° such that Φ : R°/ϖ → R°/ϖ^p, x ↦ x^p, is an isomorphism. Φ is always injective, so the condition is surjectivity, equivalently surjectivity of Frobenius on R°/p, and it is independent of ϖ. A perfectoid field is a perfectoid Tate ring which is a nonarchimedean field (by Kedlaya, Remark 6.1.8, a perfectoid Tate ring whose underlying ring is a field is one). Remark 6.1.2: perfectoid analytic Huber rings and integral perfectoid rings (BMS, Gabber–Ramero) are more general notions; the lectures' perfectoid rings are all Tate, which gives the same category of perfectoid spaces.
items.locator: Lecture 6, §6.1, Definition 6.1.1, Remark 6.1.2, Remark 6.1.3, Definition 6.1.7 and Remark 6.1.8, pp. 41–43
items.note: PerfectoidSpaces P1 nodes perfectoid-tate-rings-and-algebras, frobenius-surjectivity-criterion and perfectoid-ring-field-is-perfectoid-field.

items.name: Remark 6.1.4, Example 6.1.5, Proposition 6.1.6 and Proposition 6.1.9: examples and characterizations of perfectoid rings
items.statement: ℚ_p and discretely valued fields are not perfectoid. ℚ_p^cycl, 𝔽_p((t^{1/p^∞})), ℚ_p^cycl⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩ and ℤ_p^cycl[[T^{1/p^∞}]]⟨(p/T)^{1/p^∞}⟩[1/T] are perfectoid. A complete Tate ring with pR = 0 is perfectoid iff it is perfect. A nonarchimedean field K is perfectoid iff it is not discretely valued, |p| < 1, and Φ : 𝒪_K/p → 𝒪_K/p is surjective.
items.locator: Lecture 6, §6.1, Remark 6.1.4, Example 6.1.5, Proposition 6.1.6 and Proposition 6.1.9, pp. 42–43
items.note: P1 nodes perfectoid-examples, perfect-complete-tate-ring-is-uniform, perfectoid-tate-ring-is-reduced and perfectoid-field-characterisation.

items.name: Theorem 6.1.10: rational localizations of perfectoid pairs are perfectoid (hence sheafy)
items.statement: For a Huber pair (R, R⁺) with R perfectoid, 𝒪_X(U) is perfectoid for every rational U ⊂ Spa(R, R⁺); so (R, R⁺) is stably uniform and sheafy by Theorem 5.2.5 (Scholze 2012, 6.3; Kedlaya–Liu 3.6.14). The hard part, uniformity of 𝒪_X(U), uses tilting.
items.note: P2 node perfectoid-stably-uniform-and-sheafy.

items.name: Definition 6.2.1, Lemma 6.2.2 and Remark 6.2.3: the tilt R♭
items.statement: For perfectoid R, R♭ = lim_{x ↦ x^p} R with the inverse-limit topology and addition (x^{(i)}) + (y^{(i)}) = (lim_n (x^{(i+n)} + y^{(i+n)})^{p^n}); it is a perfect complete Tate 𝔽_p-algebra with R♭° = lim_{x ↦ x^p} R° ≅ lim_Φ R°/p ≅ lim_Φ R°/ϖ. There is a pseudo-uniformizer ϖ with ϖ^p | p having compatible p-power roots; ϖ♭ = (ϖ, ϖ^{1/p}, …) is a pseudo-uniformizer of R♭ and R♭ = R♭°[1/ϖ♭]. For a perfectoid field K, K♭ (Fontaine) is a nonarchimedean field with |f| = |f♯|.
items.locator: Lecture 6, §6.2, Definition 6.2.1, Lemma 6.2.2 and Remark 6.2.3, pp. 43–44
items.note: P1 nodes tilt-of-perfectoid-tate-ring, tilt-is-perfectoid-tate-ring, tilt-integral-subrings, pseudouniformizer-with-compatible-roots, exists-pseudouniformizer-with-compatible-roots and tilt-of-perfectoid-field.

items.name: Example 6.2.4 and Lemma 6.2.5: the tilt of ℚ_p^cycl, the sharp map, and rings of integral elements under tilting
items.statement: (ℚ_p^cycl)♭ = 𝔽_p((t^{1/p^∞})) with t = (1, ζ_p, ζ_{p²}, …) − 1, the ℤ_p^×-action being γ(t) = (1 + t)^γ − 1. f ↦ f♯ (projection to the zeroth coordinate) is continuous multiplicative and induces R♭°/ϖ♭ ≅ R°/ϖ. Rings of integral elements R⁺ ⊂ R° correspond bijectively to R♭⁺ ⊂ R♭° via R♭⁺ = lim_{x ↦ x^p} R⁺, with R♭⁺/ϖ♭ = R⁺/ϖ.
items.note: P1 nodes cyclotomic-perfectoid-field and rings-of-integral-elements-under-tilting.

items.name: Theorem 6.2.6 and Theorem 7.1.1: the tilting homeomorphism of adic spectra
items.statement: For a perfectoid Huber pair (R, R⁺) with tilt (R♭, R♭⁺), (R, R⁺) is sheafy and x ↦ x♭, |f(x♭)| = |f♯(x)|, is a homeomorphism Spa(R, R⁺) ≅ Spa(R♭, R♭⁺) preserving rational subsets; for rational U with image U♭, 𝒪_X(U) is perfectoid with tilt 𝒪_{X♭}(U♭) (Kedlaya–Liu; Scholze 2012).
items.note: P2 nodes perfectoid-stably-uniform-and-sheafy and rational-localization-of-perfectoid-affinoids; AdicSpacesPartII R5 node sousperfectoid-rational-localisation.

items.name: Theorem 6.2.7: the tilting equivalence for perfectoid algebras
items.statement: For perfectoid R with tilt R♭, S ↦ S♭ is an equivalence between perfectoid R-algebras and perfectoid R♭-algebras (Kedlaya–Liu; Scholze 2012).
items.note: P1 nodes tilting-equivalence-and-explicit-tilt and tilt-functoriality.

items.name: Lemma 6.2.8, Definition 6.2.9, Lemma 6.2.10 and Theorem 6.2.11: untilts and primitive ideals of degree one
items.statement: For an untilt (R♯, R♯⁺) of a perfectoid pair (R, R⁺) (a perfectoid Tate ring with R♯♭ ≅ R identifying plus rings): θ : W(R⁺) → R♯⁺, Σ[r_n]p^n ↦ Σ r_n♯p^n, is surjective, with kernel generated by a nonzerodivisor ξ = p + [ϖ]α (ϖ ∈ R⁺ a pseudo-uniformizer, α ∈ W(R⁺)); an untilt need not have characteristic 0 (ξ = p gives R itself). An ideal of W(R⁺) is primitive of degree 1 if generated by such a ξ, and every such ξ is a nonzerodivisor. Perfectoid Tate–Huber pairs (S, S⁺) are equivalent to triples (R, R⁺, J) with (R, R⁺) perfectoid of characteristic p and J ⊂ W(R⁺) primitive of degree 1, via (S, S⁺) ↦ (S♭, S♭⁺, ker θ) and (R, R⁺, J) ↦ (W(R⁺)[[ϖ]^{-1}]/J, W(R⁺)/J) (Kedlaya–Liu; Fontaine).
items.locator: Lecture 6, §6.2, Lemma 6.2.8, Definition 6.2.9, Lemma 6.2.10 and Theorem 6.2.11, pp. 45–47
items.note: P1 nodes marked-untilt, fontaine-theta-and-primitive-kernel, distinguished-element-criterion, untilt-construction and untilts-classified-by-primitive-ideals; RF2:untilts node primitive-untilt-correspondence.

items.name: Definition 6.3.1, Example 6.3.2 and Propositions 6.3.3–6.3.4: sousperfectoid rings
items.statement: A complete Tate ℤ_p-algebra R is sousperfectoid if there is a perfectoid Tate ring R̃ with R ↪ R̃ split as topological R-modules (e.g. perfectoid rings; ℚ_p⟨T⟩ ⊂ ℚ_p^cycl⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩). If R is sousperfectoid then so are 𝒪_X(U) for rational U, finite étale R-algebras and R⟨T_1, …, T_n⟩, and every Tate–Huber pair (R, R⁺) with R sousperfectoid is stably uniform, hence sheafy.
items.locator: Lecture 6, §6.3, Definition 6.3.1, Example 6.3.2, Proposition 6.3.3 and Proposition 6.3.4, pp. 47–48
items.note: AdicSpacesPartII R5 nodes sousperfectoid-ring(s), sousperfectoid-p-adic-field, sousperfectoid-rational-localisation, sousperfectoid-finite-etale, perfectoid-times-polydisc, split-injection-completed-base-change and sousperfectoid-stably-uniform; PerfectoidSpaces P3 node perfectoid-tate-rings-are-strongly-sheafy.

items.name: Definition 7.1.2, Remark 7.1.3 and Theorem 7.1.4: perfectoid spaces and the geometric tilting equivalence
items.statement: A perfectoid space is an adic space covered by affinoids Spa(R, R⁺) with R perfectoid ('affinoid perfectoid' always means such a Spa(R, R⁺); whether a sheafy Tate pair with perfectoid spectrum has R perfectoid is open outside characteristic p). Tilting glues to X ↦ X♭, and for any perfectoid X, Y ↦ Y♭ is an equivalence between perfectoid spaces over X and over X♭.
items.locator: Lecture 7, §7.1, Definition 7.1.2, Remark 7.1.3 and Theorem 7.1.4, p. 49
items.note: P2 nodes perfectoid-space, affinoid-perfectoid-space, perfectoid-spaces-and-glued-tilting and tilting-slice-equivalence.

items.name: Theorem 7.3.1: Fontaine–Wintenberger for perfectoid fields
items.statement: For a perfectoid field K with tilt K♭: every finite extension L/K is perfectoid, and L ↦ L♭ is a degree-preserving equivalence between finite extensions of K and of K♭; hence Gal(K̄/K) ≅ Gal(K̄♭/K♭).
items.note: P3 node fontaine-wintenberger.

items.name: Theorem 7.3.2 and Example 7.3.3: finite extensions of perfectoid fields are almost étale (Tate)
items.statement: For a perfectoid field K and finite L/K, 𝒪_L/𝒪_K is almost finite étale (Tate; Gabber–Ramero 6.6); Tate proved tr(𝒪_L) ⊃ 𝔪_K for some such K. For K = ℚ_p(p^{1/p^∞})^∧ and L = K(√p) (p ≠ 2), the differents of K_n(√p)/K_n have valuation 1/(2p^n) → 0.
items.note: P3 nodes almost-finite-etale-equivalence and finite-extensions-of-perfectoid-fields.

items.name: Definitions 7.4.1 and 7.4.3 with Example 7.4.2: almost mathematics
items.statement: An R°-module M is almost zero if ϖM = 0 for all pseudo-uniformizers ϖ (equivalently ϖ^{1/p^n}M = 0 for all n, for a fixed ϖ with p-power roots); similarly for R⁺-modules. The residue field of a perfectoid field is almost zero, R°/R⁺ is almost zero, almost zero modules form a thick Serre subcategory, and the almost category R°a-mod is the quotient (and equivalent to R⁺a-mod).
items.locator: Lecture 7, §7.4, Definition 7.4.1, Example 7.4.2 and Definition 7.4.3, p. 52
items.note: P0 nodes almost-zero-serre-class and change-of-basic-setup.

items.name: Theorem 7.4.4: almost acyclicity of 𝒪⁺ on affinoid perfectoids
items.statement: For a perfectoid Tate–Huber pair (R, R⁺) and X = Spa(R, R⁺), H^i(X, 𝒪_X⁺) is almost zero for i > 0 and H^0(X, 𝒪_X⁺) = R⁺ (and H^i(X, 𝒪_X) = 0 for i > 0 by Kedlaya–Liu).
items.note: P2 nodes integral-almost-acyclicity, integral-cech-cohomology-bounded-torsion and sheaf-theorem-and-almost-acyclicity; P0 nodes almost-cech-acyclicity-criterion and almost-cech-and-sheaf-cohomology.

items.name: Theorem 7.4.5, Lemma 7.4.6 and Theorem 7.4.8: almost purity and the tilting of finite étale algebras
items.statement: For perfectoid R with tilt R♭: (1) every finite étale R-algebra S is perfectoid; (2) S ↦ S♭ is an equivalence of finite étale R- and R♭-algebras; (3) (almost purity) S° is almost finite étale over R° (Faltings; Kedlaya–Liu; Scholze). The proof passes to residue fields: 2-colim_{U ∋ x} {finite étale 𝒪_X(U)-algebras} ≅ {finite étale K(x)-algebras} (7.4.6), which rests on (7.4.8, Elkik, Gabber–Ramero): for a topologically henselian Tate ring A, B ↦ B ⊗_A Â is an equivalence of finite étale algebras, so for complete Tate A_i, 2-colim {finite étale A_i-algebras} ≅ {finite étale colim A_i-algebras} ≅ {finite étale (colim A_i)^∧-algebras} (Remark 7.4.7 defines filtered 2-colimits of categories).
items.locator: Lecture 7, §7.4, Theorem 7.4.5, Lemma 7.4.6, Remark 7.4.7 and Theorem 7.4.8, pp. 53–54

items.name: Definition 7.5.1, Proposition 7.5.2 and Corollary 7.5.3: finite étale and étale morphisms of perfectoid spaces and the étale site
items.statement: f : X → Y is finite étale if over every affinoid Spa(B, B⁺) ⊂ Y, X ×_Y Spa(B, B⁺) = Spa(A, A⁺) with A finite étale over B and A⁺ the integral closure of B⁺; f is étale if locally it factors as an open immersion followed by a finite étale map; étale covers are jointly surjective families. (Finite) étale maps are stable under composition and pullback, satisfy cancellation (g, gf étale ⇒ f étale), and f is (finite) étale iff f♭ is. Hence X_ét ≅ X♭_ét, and H^i(X_ét, 𝒪_X⁺) is almost zero for i > 0 on affinoid X.
items.locator: Lecture 7, §7.5, Definition 7.5.1, Proposition 7.5.2 and Corollary 7.5.3, p. 55

items.name: Definition 8.2.1, Example 8.2.2, Remark 8.2.3 and Lemma 8.2.4: pro-étale morphisms of perfectoid spaces
items.statement: A map Spa(B, B⁺) → Spa(A, A⁺) of affinoid perfectoid spaces is affinoid pro-étale if (B, B⁺) is the completed filtered colimit of perfectoid (A_i, A_i⁺) étale over Spa(A, A⁺); f : X → Y is pro-étale if it is locally affinoid pro-étale. For a profinite (or locally profinite) set S, X × S = lim X × S_i → X is pro-étale; pro-étale maps need not be open. For affinoid pro-étale presentations, Hom_{Spa(A,A⁺)}(Spa(A_∞, A_∞⁺), Spa(B_∞, B_∞⁺)) = lim_J colim_I Hom(Spa(A_i, A_i⁺), Spa(B_j, B_j⁺)) (Scholze 2017, 7.10).
items.locator: Lecture 8, §8.2, Definition 8.2.1, Example 8.2.2, Remark 8.2.3 and Lemma 8.2.4, p. 57

items.name: Proposition 8.2.5: stability of pro-étale maps, and fibre products of perfectoid spaces
items.statement: Compositions and pullbacks of pro-étale maps are pro-étale, and if g and h = g ∘ f are pro-étale then f is (Scholze 2017, 7.11); the category of affinoid perfectoid spaces has all connected limits, so fibre products of perfectoid spaces exist. Being pro-étale is not pro-étale local on the target.
items.note: P6 nodes pro-etale-stability-and-limits, affinoid-pro-etale-cofiltered-limits and kappa-small-closure; P2 node fibre-products-of-perfectoid-spaces.

items.name: Definition 8.2.6 and Remark 8.2.7: the big pro-étale sites Perfd, Perf and X_proét
items.statement: On Perfd (perfectoid spaces), Perf (those of characteristic p) and X_proét (perfectoid spaces pro-étale over X), a family {f_i : Y_i → Y} is a pro-étale cover if the f_i are pro-étale and every quasicompact open U ⊂ Y is the union of the images of finitely many quasicompact opens U_i ⊂ Y_i. Topological surjectivity alone is not enough (a profinite set covered by its points).
items.note: DiamondsAndVStacks D2 ('Use the actual covering condition … Mere point-surjectivity … is not the definition'); set-theoretic cutoffs as in Scholze 2017.

items.name: Proposition 8.2.8: 𝒪 and 𝒪⁺ are pro-étale sheaves, and the pro-étale site is subcanonical
items.statement: For a perfectoid space X, the presheaves Y ↦ 𝒪_Y(Y), 𝒪_Y⁺(Y) on Perfd are sheaves; for affinoid X, H^i(X_proét, 𝒪_X) = 0 and H^i(X_proét, 𝒪_X⁺) is almost zero for i > 0; and every representable presheaf h_X is a pro-étale sheaf (Scholze 2017, 8.6).
items.note: D2 ('Prove that 𝒪 and 𝒪⁺ are … sheaves'); P0 nodes almost-exactness-passes-to-completion and almost-inversion-and-completion.

items.name: Definition 8.3.1, Remark 8.3.2, Definition/Proposition 8.3.3 and Proposition 8.3.4: diamonds
items.statement: A diamond is a pro-étale sheaf D on Perf of the form X/R, X a perfectoid space of characteristic p and R ⊂ X × X an equivalence relation that is a perfectoid space with pro-étale projections (compare algebraic spaces). A map f : Y → X of perfectoid spaces is an injection if the equivalent conditions hold: Hom(T, Y) → Hom(T, X) injective for all T; injective on (K, K⁺)-points; injective on (C, C⁺)-points, C algebraically closed; |Y| → |X| injective with K(y) ≅ K(x); |Y| → |X| injective and Hom(T, Y) = Hom(T, X) ×_{C^0(|T|,|X|)} C^0(|T|, |Y|) (Scholze 2017, 5.3). If R ⇉ X are pro-étale and R → X × X is an injective equivalence relation, D = X/R is a diamond with R ≅ X ×_D X (Scholze 2017, 11.3).
items.locator: Lecture 8, §8.3, Definition 8.3.1, Remark 8.3.2, Definition/Proposition 8.3.3 and Proposition 8.3.4, pp. 60–61
items.note: DiamondsAndVStacks D4 ('Define a diamond by a pro-étale sheaf quotient U/R … Prove effectiveness of the relation'); injections of perfectoid spaces are PerfectoidSpaces P4 material (ECD §5).

items.name: Lemma 8.3.5, Remark 8.3.6 and Proposition 8.3.7: absolute products
items.statement: The absolute product of two perfectoid spaces of characteristic p is perfectoid (Perf has no final object, so this is not a fibre product), and the product sheaf D × D′ of diamonds is a diamond.
items.locator: Lecture 8, §8.3, Lemma 8.3.5, Remark 8.3.6 and Proposition 8.3.7, pp. 61–62
items.note: P2 node products-in-perf; D4 ('products, fibre products').

items.name: Example 8.1.1, Proposition 8.4.1 and Theorem 8.4.2: the functor of points of Spd ℚ_p
items.statement: For X = Spa(R, R⁺) affinoid perfectoid of characteristic p, (Spd ℚ_p)(X) is the set of isomorphism classes of pairs: a ℤ_p^×-torsor R → R̃ = (colim R_n)^∧ with R_n/R finite étale Galois with group (ℤ/p^n)^×, and a topologically nilpotent unit t ∈ R̃ with γ(t) = (1 + t)^γ − 1. The category of perfectoid spaces over ℚ_p is equivalent to that of perfectoid spaces X of characteristic p with a map X → Spd ℚ_p.
items.locator: Lecture 8, §8.4, Proposition 8.4.1 and Theorem 8.4.2 with Example 8.1.1 (p. 56), p. 63
items.note: DiamondsAndVStacks D6 ('Construct Spd ℤ_p by marked untilts …'); the proof is §9.4 (Theorem 9.4.4).

items.name: Question 9.1.1, Example 9.1.2 and Theorem 9.1.3: pro-étale descent of perfectoid spaces
items.statement: Pro-étale descent of morphisms of perfectoid spaces is not effective in general (there is no good notion of affinoid morphism in rigid geometry: V = {|x| = 1 or |y| = 1} ⊂ Spa K⟨x, y⟩ is not affinoid, H^1(V, 𝒪_V) ≠ 0, although it is rational on each piece of a rational cover). It is effective along a pro-étale cover X′ → X for Y′ → X′ when (1) X, X′, Y′ are affinoid and X is totally disconnected; (2) Y′ → X′ is separated pro-étale and X strictly totally disconnected; (3) Y′ → X′ is separated étale; (4) Y′ → X′ is finite étale; the descended map has the same properties (Scholze 2017, 9.3, 9.6, 9.7).
items.locator: Lecture 9, §9.1, Question 9.1.1, Example 9.1.2 and Theorem 9.1.3, pp. 64–65
items.note: DiamondsAndVStacks D3 ('Prove ECD 9.2–9.11 … The effectivity assertions have distinct scopes').

items.name: Proposition 9.1.4 and Example 9.1.5: locally pro-étale maps and the punctual criterion
items.statement: For f : X → Y a map of affinoid perfectoid spaces, TFAE: there is an affinoid pro-étale surjection Y′ → Y with X ×_Y Y′ → Y′ affinoid pro-étale; for every rank-one geometric point Spa C → Y, X ×_Y Spa C ≅ Spa C × S for a profinite set S (Scholze 2017, 7.19). Spa K⟨T^{1/2p^∞}⟩ → Spa K⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩ (p ≠ 2) is of this kind but not pro-étale.
items.note: D1 (classification of separated qc pro-étale maps over strictly totally disconnected bases) and D3 (quasi-pro-étale morphisms).

items.name: Definition 9.1.6: totally disconnected and strictly totally disconnected perfectoid spaces
items.statement: A perfectoid space is totally disconnected (resp. strictly totally disconnected) if it is qcqs and every open (resp. étale) cover splits. Totally disconnected spaces are affinoid, with connected components Spa(K, K⁺) for perfectoid affinoid fields, K algebraically closed in the strict case (Scholze 2017, 7.5).
items.note: DiamondsAndVStacks D1 ('Distinguish totally disconnected, strictly totally disconnected …').

items.name: Definitions 9.2.1–9.2.2 and Proposition 9.2.3: quasi-pro-étale maps and the atlas characterization of diamonds
items.statement: f : X → Y of perfectoid spaces is quasi-pro-étale if its pullback to every strictly totally disconnected Y′ → Y is pro-étale (equivalently the criterion of 9.1.4 on affinoids). A map F → G of pro-étale sheaves on Perf is quasi-pro-étale if it is locally separated and its pullback to every strictly totally disconnected Y → G is representable by a perfectoid space pro-étale over Y. A pro-étale sheaf is a diamond iff it admits a surjective quasi-pro-étale map from a perfectoid space (Scholze 2017, 11.5).
items.locator: Lecture 9, §9.2, Definition 9.2.1, Definition 9.2.2 and Proposition 9.2.3, p. 67
items.note: D3 ('Define étale, finite étale and quasi-pro-étale morphisms of stacks as in ECD 10.1') and D4 ('the quasi-pro-étale atlas characterization').

items.name: Proposition 9.3.1 and Remark 9.3.2: pro-étale torsors under profinite groups
items.statement: For a G-torsor F′ → F, G profinite, and affinoid X = Spa(B, B⁺) → F, F′ ×_F X is an affinoid perfectoid Spa(A, A⁺) with A the completion of colim_H A_H, A_H/B a finite étale G/H-torsor (A_H = A^H) (Scholze 2017, 10.13, which also treats locally profinite G).
items.note: D3/D4 (torsors and quotient stability); AdicEtaleGeometry A4 node finite-etale-galois-torsor for the Galois-tower case.

items.name: Definition 9.4.1, Lemma 9.4.2 and Corollary 9.4.3: Spd ℚ_p as Spa(ℚ_p^cycl)♭/ℤ_p^×
items.statement: Spd ℚ_p = Spa(ℚ_p^cycl)♭/ℤ_p^×, the coequalizer of ℤ_p^× × Spa(ℚ_p^cycl)♭ ⇉ Spa(ℚ_p^cycl)♭ (projection and action); the map ℤ_p^× × Spd ℚ_p^cycl → Spd ℚ_p^cycl × Spd ℚ_p^cycl is an injection, Spa ℚ_p^cycl → Spd ℚ_p is a ℤ_p^×-torsor, and Proposition 8.4.1 holds.
items.locator: Lecture 9, §9.4, Definition 9.4.1, Lemma 9.4.2 and Corollary 9.4.3, p. 70
items.note: D6 and AdicEtaleGeometry A4 node perfectoid-cover-presentation.

items.name: Theorem 9.4.4, Lemma 9.4.5 and Remark 9.4.6: perfectoid spaces over ℚ_p are characteristic-p perfectoid spaces over Spd ℚ_p
items.statement: Perfectoid spaces over ℚ_p are equivalent to perfectoid spaces of characteristic p with a map to Spd ℚ_p: both are fibred over Perf with no nontrivial automorphisms, and the presheaf Untilt_{ℚ_p} (X ↦ {(X♯, ι : X♯♭ ≅ X)}) is a pro-étale sheaf on Perf (Scholze 2017, 15.1(i)) isomorphic to Spd ℚ_p. Any perfectoid K/ℚ_p that is the completion of an algebraic extension may replace ℚ_p^cycl.
items.locator: Lecture 9, §9.4, Theorem 9.4.4, Lemma 9.4.5 and Remark 9.4.6, pp. 70–73
items.note: D6 ('prove functorial pullback from the tilting equivalence, absence of automorphisms, and v-descent').

items.name: Definitions 10.1.1 and 10.1.3 with Remarks 10.1.2 and 10.1.4: the functor X ↦ X^♦ and Spd ℤ_p
items.statement: For an analytic pre-adic space X over Spa ℤ_p, X^♦(T) is the set of isomorphism classes of pairs (T♯, T♯ → X), T♯ an untilt of the characteristic-p perfectoid space T; Spd(R, R⁺) := Spa(R, R⁺)^♦. For perfectoid X, X^♦ = X♭. Spd ℤ_p = Untilt, the presheaf of untilts S♯ of S over ℤ_p (always including the trivial untilt (S, id)); it is a pro-étale sheaf but not a diamond.
items.locator: Lecture 10, §10.1, Definition 10.1.1, Remark 10.1.2, Definition 10.1.3 and Remark 10.1.4, p. 74
items.note: D6 ('Construct Spd ℤ_p by marked untilts … Construct Spd(A,A⁺) for a Tate ℤ_p-pair … Distinguish a Tate pair from an arbitrary formal base such as (ℤ_p,ℤ_p)').

items.name: Theorem 10.1.5 with Lemmas 10.1.6–10.1.7: X^♦ is a diamond
items.statement: For an analytic pre-adic space X over ℤ_p, X^♦ is a diamond (Scholze 2017, 15.6). (10.1.6, Faltings, Colmez, Scholze 2017 15.3) If R is a Tate ring with p topologically nilpotent and colim R_i a filtered colimit of finite étale R-algebras with no nonsplit finite étale covers, topologized so that colim R_i° is open and bounded, its completion R̃ is perfectoid. (10.1.7) Spd(R, R⁺) = Spd(R̃, R̃⁺)/G with Spd(R̃, R̃⁺) → Spd(R, R⁺) a G-torsor; in particular Spd(R, R⁺) is a diamond.
items.locator: Lecture 10, §10.1, Theorem 10.1.5, Lemma 10.1.6 and Lemma 10.1.7, p. 75

items.name: Example 10.1.8: Spd ℚ_p × Spd ℚ_p as (D̃*_{ℚ_p})^♦/ℤ_p^×
items.statement: With D_{ℚ_p} ⊂ 𝔾_m via x ↦ 1 + x and D̃*_{ℚ_p} the punctured perfectoid open disc (inverse limit along p-th powers), there is an isomorphism of diamonds (D̃*_{ℚ_p})^♦/ℤ_p^× ≅ Spd ℚ_p × Spd ℚ_p over the first projection, deduced from a ℤ_p^× × ℤ_p^×-equivariant isomorphism (D̃*_{ℚ_p^cycl})^♦ ≅ Spd ℚ_p^cycl × Spd ℚ_p^cycl.

items.name: Proposition 10.2.1 and Lemma 10.2.2: universal homeomorphisms give isomorphic diamonds
items.statement: If f : X → X′ is a universal homeomorphism of analytic pre-adic spaces over Spa ℚ_p, then f^♦ : X^♦ → X′^♦ is an isomorphism; the proof shows 𝒪_{X′}⁺/p^n → 𝒪_X⁺/p^n is an isomorphism of sheaves on |X| = |X′|.

items.name: Proposition 10.2.3: full faithfulness on seminormal rigid-analytic spaces
items.statement: For a nonarchimedean field K over ℚ_p, X ↦ X^♦ is fully faithful from seminormal rigid-analytic spaces over K to diamonds over Spd K (the structure map to Spd K must be remembered).

items.name: Definition 10.3.1, Remarks 10.3.2–10.3.3, Proposition 10.3.4, Definition 10.3.5 and Propositions 10.3.6–10.3.7: the underlying space of a diamond
items.statement: For a presentation D = X/R, |D| = |X|/|R| (independent of the presentation; Scholze 2017, 11.14); quasicompact diamonds are not stable under products (X × X for X = Spa 𝔽_p((t^{1/p^∞})) is not quasicompact). For qcqs D, |D| is T_0. A map G → F of pro-étale sheaves is an open immersion if every pullback to a perfectoid space is an open subspace; open subsheaves of a diamond F correspond to open subsets of |F| (Scholze 2017, 11.15), and for an analytic pre-adic space X over ℤ_p, |X^♦| ≅ |X| (Scholze 2017, 15.6).

items.name: Definition 10.4.1, Theorem 10.4.2 and Proposition 10.4.3: étale maps of diamonds and the site comparison
items.statement: A map G → F of pro-étale sheaves on Perf is (finite) étale if it is locally separated and every pullback to a perfectoid space X is a perfectoid space (finite) étale over X. X ↦ X^♦ induces equivalences X_ét ≅ X^♦_ét and X_fét ≅ X^♦_fét for analytic pre-adic X over ℤ_p (Scholze 2017, 15.6); X_qproét := X^♦_qproét is a replete topos, and ν_X^* : X_ét^∼ → X_qproét^∼ is fully faithful (Scholze 2017, 14.8).
items.locator: Lecture 10, §10.4, Definition 10.4.1, Theorem 10.4.2 and Proposition 10.4.3, pp. 80–81

items.name: Theorem 10.5.1 (Appendix to Lecture 10): R^if_*𝔽_p is a local system for proper smooth maps
items.statement: Let C be a complete algebraically closed extension of ℚ_p and f : X → Y a proper smooth map of rigid-analytic spaces over C. For an étale 𝔽_p-local system 𝕃 on X, every R^if_*𝕃 is an étale 𝔽_p-local system on Y. This removes the extra hypothesis of Scholze, p-adic Hodge theory for rigid-analytic varieties, Theorem 1.10 (the ℤ_p version follows formally).

items.name: Proposition 10.5.2, Lemma 10.5.3 and Remark 10.5.5: coherence of R⁺/ϖ over totally disconnected spaces
items.statement: For a totally disconnected perfectoid Spa(R, R⁺) and a pseudouniformizer ϖ, R⁺/ϖ is coherent, hence almost coherent (almost finitely generated submodules of almost finitely presented modules are almost finitely presented; M is almost finitely generated/presented if for every pseudouniformizer ε there are M → M_ε → M, M_ε finitely generated/presented, composing to ε in both directions). If H^i(X_S, 𝕃 ⊗ 𝒪⁺_{X_S}/p) is an almost finitely presented R⁺/p-module over a strictly totally disconnected S → Y, then (R^if_*𝕃)|_S, and hence R^if_*𝕃, is an 𝔽_p-local system. (Almost finitely presented R⁺/p-modules are almost locally constant over a constructible stratification of Spa(R, R⁺), unlike finitely presented R-modules over Spec R.)
items.locator: Appendix to Lecture 10, §10.5, Proposition 10.5.2, Lemma 10.5.3, Remark 10.5.4 and Remark 10.5.5, p. 84

items.name: Lemmas 10.5.6, 10.5.8, 10.5.9 and Proposition 10.5.10: the Cartan–Serre argument over a strictly totally disconnected base
items.statement: (10.5.6) For upper-right-quadrant spectral sequences E_{*,(i)} ⇒ M_{(i)}, i = 0, …, (N+1)3^{N+1}, with maps whose r-th-sheet components factor over almost finitely presented R⁺/p-modules, M^k_{(0)} → M^k_{((N+1)3^{N+1})} factors over an almost finitely presented module for k ≤ N. (10.5.8) For V = Spa(B, B⁺) → 𝔹^n_S a composite of rational embeddings and finite étale maps and a rational U = Spa(A, A⁺) ⊂ V strictly contained in V relative to S, B⁺/p → A⁺/p factors over a finitely presented R⁺/p-module; (10.5.9) A⁺/p is a finitely presented R⁺/p-algebra for such U. (10.5.10) H^i(X_S, 𝕃 ⊗ 𝒪⁺_{X_S}/p) is an almost finitely presented R⁺/p-module, proving Theorem 10.5.1.
